model.label: Government-run social health insurance in two main schemes (compulsory for employees, voluntary and subsidised for other residents), with medical assistance for the poor

overview.statement: China began its current round of health reform in 2009 with the aim of giving everyone basic health care coverage by the end of 2020.

Public coverage was built on three basic schemes: one for urban employees, one for rural residents (NRCMS) and one for non-employed urban residents (URBMI). In 2016 the government merged the two residents' schemes into a single urban and rural residents' scheme, and in 2018 it created the National Healthcare Security Administration to run the schemes under one body.

locator.section: Main reform initiatives: health insurance system

overview.statement: With the 2009 reform, China committed to equal access to basic health care of reasonable quality with financial protection for all citizens, and the government has since increased its health funding fourfold.

The residents' scheme covers nearly 960 million people, about 80% of them rural residents, while around 5% of the population (nearly 50 million people) is uninsured, according to the sources this 2025 study cites.

The residents' scheme is open to every urban and rural resident not covered by employee insurance. Employee insurance is compulsory by law and funded partly by employers, while joining the residents' scheme is voluntary.

financing.statement: Residents pay a flat yearly contribution that has risen from 10 yuan per person when rural insurance began in 2003 to 380 yuan by 2024, while rural residents' disposable income averaged 23,119 yuan in 2024; interviewees described the rising contributions as a heavy burden for rural families.

As described in the 2015 WHO/Asia Pacific Observatory review, all urban employers and their employees, including retirees, must join the employee scheme, with contributions of at least 2% of salary from the employee and 6% from the employer.

locator.section: 3.3 Sources of revenue: social insurance contribution

financing.statement: The 2015 review notes that each local government, usually at the prefecture-level city, sets the actual employee-scheme contribution rate, and that retirees pay no contribution.

locator.section: 3.3 Sources of revenue: social insurance contribution

financing.statement: The 2015 review reported that the residents' schemes of that time (URBMI and NRCMS, merged from 2016) were funded by individual premiums and government money, with government subsidies the larger part.

covered.statement: By 2018, over 95% of China's population was enrolled in a social health insurance scheme.
The national insurance drug list had grown to 2,643 medicines by 2019, and per-person government subsidies for the residents' schemes in 2018 were more than five times their 2009 level.
A government-funded basic public health package is offered to nearly everyone; it grew from 9 service categories in 2009 to 14 in 2017, and funding rose from ¥15 per person in 2009 to ¥55 in 2018.
Under national procurement, the manufacturers that win a tender are guaranteed 60-70% of the previous year's total use of that drug, which gives the public payer strong leverage over prices.

Decisions on which drugs are reimbursed have become more centralised: provincial routes were removed, the National Healthcare Security Administration was created, and the National Reimbursement Drug List is now the main way a drug gets covered.

Since national price negotiations began in 2017, drugs added to the reimbursement list have taken average price cuts of 44% to 61% per annual round; in 2020, 704 drugs passed initial review, 162 were shortlisted and 119 were successfully negotiated, a 17% success rate.

locator.section: HTA decision making, reimbursement and price negotiation

covered.statement: According to the authors, listing decisions weigh a drug's innovation, added clinical benefit and cost-effectiveness against current care, the level of unmet need, and the budget impact on the basic insurance funds, much as other national health technology assessment systems do.
The social insurance schemes built from 1998 onwards for urban employees and for urban and rural residents differed in scope and mainly covered inpatient care.

cost_sharing.statement: Two supplementary layers sit on top of basic insurance: Medical Financial Assistance for people in poverty, started in 2003, and Catastrophic Medical Insurance for people with very high medical costs, started in 2012.

locator.section: Main reform initiatives: health insurance system

cost_sharing.statement: Insurance reimbursement for a procured drug is set by the winning bid's price: patients who take the winning manufacturer's product pay a small share, while those who choose another version pay the difference in price themselves.

According to the 2015 review, the basic schemes reimburse eligible hospital costs and outpatient costs for severe diseases subject to deductibles, co-payments and annual ceilings; insured people pay out of pocket for items outside the reimbursement list, deductibles, co-payments and costs above the ceiling.

Local governments have wide latitude over outpatient cover, so deductibles, reimbursement rates and caps vary by place; Beijing and Shanghai began outpatient cover for employees in 2001, while some cities had none as late as 2018.

financial_hardship.statement: In 2018, medical assistance funds spent ¥42.46 billion nationally: they paid insurance contributions for 76.7 million people and helped 53.6 million people with outpatient and inpatient costs.
It also found that catastrophic health spending is unusually common in China compared with countries at a similar level of economic development.

A study of 28 provinces using the 2017 China Household Finance Survey estimated that 11.0% of households nationally had catastrophic health expenditure, ranging from 6.3% in Beijing to 16.0% in Heilongjiang, and that 2.0% experienced medical impoverishment, from 0.03% in Shanghai to 4.6% in Anhui.

In that study, a household had catastrophic health expenditure when its health spending in a year reached at least 40% of its total spending other than food; medical impoverishment means out-of-pocket health spending left a household below, or further below, the poverty line.

Using 2015 survey data (before the 2016 merger of the rural and urban residents' schemes) and counting only money borrowed from family, friends or third parties to pay for care, a study found medical debt in 2.42% of middle-income and 3.92% of low-income households; among low-income households the average debt was 2.49 times average yearly household income, and medical debt impoverished about 10% of non-poor households.

The authors note that with this narrow definition medical debt was relatively uncommon, but that where it occurred it was a lasting burden, pushing many low- and middle-income households into poverty and committing them to years of repayments.

additional_care.statement: Since around 2021, city-based 'inclusive commercial health insurance' plans have spread: voluntary, community-rated products with low premiums (on average under 0.28% of disposable income per person in 2021), no age or job limits and few restrictions for pre-existing conditions, paying for large costs left after basic insurance up to a ceiling of 1 million yuan.

These plans are underwritten by groups of insurers with local government help in design, promotion and data sharing; by the end of 2021 they ran in 244 prefecture-level cities with about 140 million cumulative enrolments, but national enrolment was only around 5%, too low for a sustainable risk pool.

Long-term care insurance began in Qingdao in 2012 and was piloted in further cities in 2016 and 2018; by the end of 2022 the pilot cities had 16.99 million members and 12.08 million people receiving benefits.

access.statement: Between 2012 and 2017, the primary care workforce grew by 7.1% to 3.863 million, and general practitioners rose from 0.8 to 1.8 per 10,000 people.

Primary care providers are usually neither patients' first point of contact nor coordinators of specialist care; primary care facilities handled 53% of outpatient visits in 2018, down from 62% in 2010, despite the 2009 reform's push to strengthen them.
The 2015 review found no gatekeeping: patients can go directly to any hospital, which crowds tertiary hospitals while primary care is underused.
The 2015 review described general practice as still in its infancy and severely short-staffed, with 109,794 GPs in 2012.
The number of general practitioners in mainland China grew from 109,794 in 2012 to 434,868 in 2021, or 3.08 per 10,000 people.
GPs remain unevenly spread across regions; the western region has too few relative both to its population and to its land area.

outcomes.statement: In the GBD 2016 Healthcare Access and Quality (HAQ) Index, China sat in the eighth of ten deciles nationally, but its provinces ranged from the top decile (Beijing, 91.5) to the fourth (Tibet, 48.0), with eastern provinces scoring higher than western ones.
Between 1990 and 2016, China was among the middle-income countries with the largest gains in the HAQ Index, which measures deaths from causes that timely, effective health care should prevent.

A composite index of management of non-communicable diseases (eight service and risk-factor indicators) rose only slowly, from 62.0% in 2004 to 64.3% in 2018, with prevention lagging; all the indicators were unlikely to reach their 2030 targets.
Rural areas consistently had fewer health resources than urban areas and scored 2.2% lower on management of non-communicable diseases in 2018.

costs.statement: In 2017, drugs and consumables made up 48.0% of public hospitals' revenue (medicines alone 34.7%), while payment for medical staff services was 27.5%.
Between 2008 and 2018, government funding for primary care institutions grew more than tenfold, reaching ¥197 billion (it had been ¥19 billion).
By the end of 2021, national volume-based procurement had saved more than 260 billion yuan (about US$36.3 billion), according to the figures the authors cite.
Government health spending rose from 24.7% of total health spending in 2008 to 30.4% in 2020, and from 4.4% to 7.8% of all government spending over the same period.

China's total health spending passed 9 trillion yuan in 2023; the authors report that medical costs have grown by more than 10% a year, well above growth in GDP and disposable income, and that residents' out-of-pocket costs have risen despite higher reimbursement rates.

Total out-of-pocket medical spending rose from 657 billion yuan in 2009 to 1,513 billion yuan in 2017, while its share of total health spending fell from 37.46% in 2009 to under 30% by 2015 and stayed there through 2017.

what_works.statement: A Lancet review of the decade after 2009 found major gains in equal access to care and in financial protection, with the largest gains among people of lower socioeconomic status.

A 2023 Lancet Public Health assessment found that coverage of maternal, newborn and child health, infectious disease services and service capacity and access is now comparable to high-income countries, with smaller inequalities than before.
Seven rounds of national volume-based drug procurement between 2018 and 2022 lowered the prices of 294 drug formulations by an average of 53%.

A cohort study found that, among middle-aged and older rural adults, the merger of the urban and rural residents' insurance schemes was associated with better self-rated health and fewer depressive symptoms.

A study of about 1.5 million inpatient cases in Tianjin (November 2021 to September 2022) found that hospitals in the national DRG payment pilot did more laparoscopic surgery, used fewer low-value drugs and had fewer 30-day readmissions than non-pilot hospitals.
The same analysis credits strong political commitment and targeted funding for good results in reproductive, maternal, newborn and child health and in infectious diseases.
Rates of catastrophic health spending and medical impoverishment fell significantly between 2010 and 2016, according to earlier research the study cites.

problems.statement: The same review found remaining gaps in quality of care, control of non-communicable diseases, efficiency, spending growth and public satisfaction.

The same assessment found large gaps in chronic disease services: risk-factor control has barely improved in ten years, and coverage for most chronic conditions is below that of high-income countries.

Social health insurance pays wherever patients seek care, with no referral needed, and pays more generously for hospital care than for primary care, which encourages patients to bypass primary care and leaves it unable to act as a gatekeeper.

In a study in western China using trained actors posing as patients with dysentery or angina, village doctors asked 18% of recommended questions, did 15% of recommended examinations, and correctly diagnosed 26% of cases.
Systematic reviews put the average rate of antibiotic use in primary care facilities above 50%, far above the WHO-recommended level of under 30%.

A 2020 Lancet review traced poor primary care quality to weak practitioner training, fee-for-service payment that rewards tests and treatment over prevention, separation of clinical care from public health services, and poor continuity of care.

Financial protection varies widely between provinces: income-related inequality was generally much lower within the developed eastern provinces than within central and western ones, and the authors call for particular attention to low-income households in central and western provinces.

Citing National Healthcare Security Administration data, a 2025 study reports that enrolment in the urban and rural residents' scheme fell each year from 2019, by 0.3%, 0.8%, 0.8% and then 2.5% in 2022, when it dropped by 25.17 million people.

In interviews with 42 officials, village staff and residents in one rural county, the main reasons people dropped out of insurance were heavy cost, a scheme design seen as unfair, failing enrolment campaigns, and misleading information online.

A 2020 comparison with Vietnam found that China's insurance benefit packages differed by region and scheme and depended heavily on how much was paid in, which limited service coverage in less developed areas.

The same Tianjin study linked DRG payment to longer waits for surgery (by 0.18 days), more outpatient visits in the three days before admission and after discharge, and higher 30-day all-cause mortality (up 0.28 percentage points).

A 2023 Lancet Public Health analysis attributes China's weak chronic disease control and financial protection, especially for lower-income households, to a fragmented, hospital-centred delivery system, rising costs, shallow insurance benefits, and little attention to health across other policy areas.

reforms.statement: By 2017 every public hospital in China had stopped adding a mark-up to the medicines it sells, which had been a source of hospital revenue.

By 2017, 65% of public hospitals at level two or above had begun paying by disease category under insurance, and in 2019 the government named 30 pilot cities for diagnosis-related group (DRG) payment.

From 2012 the reform's second phase turned to the delivery system: public hospital reform (ending drug-sale mark-ups, changing fee schedules, provider payment and governance) and moving away from a hospital-centred, treatment-focused model.

In 2018 the central government launched national volume-based procurement of medicines, starting with a pilot in 11 cities (the '4+7' scheme); a year later every province of mainland China had joined.

A 2021 State Council guideline on outpatient mutual-aid under the employee scheme began nationwide rollout of pooled outpatient funds, intended to give more financial support for outpatient care and lower what individuals pay.

In 2019 China launched a national program of diagnosis-related group (DRG) bundled payment for hospital admissions, announced officially in 2020 by the National Healthcare Security Administration as the CHS-DRG system.

us_lessons.statement: Writing about other low- and middle-income countries rather than the US, the authors argue that parts of China's pooled procurement can transfer (procurement targeted by market size and drug importance, several winning suppliers, and quality checks on generics), but that it depends on a strong public drug plan with large purchasing power.

A US editorial on Chinese telehealth data from 2016-2020 notes that patients in less developed regions used telehealth apps to reach doctors in better-resourced areas such as Beijing, Shanghai and Guangdong, home to 51 of China's top 100 hospitals.

The editorial argues that copying this in the US runs into state medical licensure laws, which generally allow doctors to practise only in the state that licensed them, whereas regulation of telehealth may be less strict in China.

locator.section: Expanding cardiovascular care through telemedicine (US implications)

us_lessons.statement: It concludes that the US should consider policies that expand interstate physician licensure agreements so that virtual care can reach medically underserved areas.

locator.section: Considering health equity in rural America

us_lessons.statement: The authors caution that telemedicine does not fix the underlying causes of rural health gaps, such as lower insurance coverage, low patient volumes that raise costs, and higher poverty.

locator.section: Considering health equity in rural America

us_lessons.statement: Drawing lessons for other countries from China and Vietnam, the study concludes that political commitment, sustainable funding and administrative capacity drive coverage expansion through insurance reform, and that schemes should cover essential services for every member and subsidise vulnerable groups.
